# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-18 (Extended v139)

## Setting and Time
Multiple periods spanning French Revolution to 1826. **Current narrative point (October 1831, morning, Barrière du Maine and aftermath)**: Paris—Gorbeau house (50-52, Salpêtrière district); Rue de la Verrerie (Courfeyrac's residence); Rue Plumet (Valjean's primary house); Rue de Babylone (secret passage exit); Rue de l'Homme Armé (secondary apartment); Rue de l'Ouest (secondary apartment); Luxembourg; Saint-Jacques-du-Haut-Pas church; Barrière du Maine; Rue de Sèvres; inner boulevard; Dunstead (harbor town in English provinces); Staveford; Wilwick (hill farms—Luena Stenenridge, Rozek Stenenridge); Rovus Prydenridge's location. **October 1831 dawn scene**: Few constellations in pale azure, earth black, heavens white, mysterious chill of twilight, lark carolling at height, Venus rising brilliantly behind Val-de-Grâce dome. Causeway leading to Barrière du Maine is prolongation of Rue de Sèvres, cut at right angles by inner boulevard. Environmental details: frost, rain threatened (but held off that morning), wind, smoke lies flat, bells ring for vespers, children chase hoops, dogs bark, gulls quarrel over fish heads, baker's boy late, lines at oven long, light goes early.

## Primary Locations
**RUE PLUMET HOUSE**: Single-story pavilion in deserted Rue Plumet with garden approximately one-and-a-half acres. Two ground-floor rooms, two first-floor chambers, downstairs kitchen, upstairs boudoir, attic. Behind pavilion: narrow courtyard, low building (two rooms, cellar). Secret-spring door masked in building communicates via long narrow paved winding corridor to Rue de Babylone quarter-league distant. Originally built mid-last-century by Paris Parliament chief justice as mistress-house; October 1829: Valjean hired and repaired as M. Fauchelevent. **Garden characteristics**: Left uncultivated; breathes melancholy, solitude, liberty, absence of man, presence of God; ancient padlocked gate twisted, tottering; nature filled with shade arranged for love. **Access strategy**: Valjean, Cosette, Toussaint enter/emerge only via Rue de Babylone door.

**POOR MEADOWS NEAR BARRIÈRE DU MAINE**: Nearly confounded with city; grow sickly grain in summer; after autumn harvest appear peeled rather than reaped. Solitary, beloved by Valjean for freedom and privacy it offers Cosette.

## Jean Valjean's Crisis and Altered Routine (April Year 4 through October 1831)
**The ambush aftermath**: M. Leblanc (Cosette's biological father) escaped unscrewing coin piece and cutting cords; Javert positioned outside, captured Thénardier and gang. Valjean subsequently relocated with Cosette to Rue Plumet (October 1829) as M. Fauchelevent.

**Valjean and Marius conflict (Spring-Summer Year 5)**: Marius initially indifferent toward Cosette, then began paying attention (wearing new coat daily, uncertain if hair curled, wearing gloves, exhibiting awkward unnatural behavior). Valjean detected these changes and instituted undeclared war: changed hours, changed benches, forgot handkerchief, came alone to Luxembourg, laid ambushes. Marius dashed headlong into all snares. Cosette remained immured in apparent unconcern. Valjean cordially detested Marius; experienced moments when thought becoming savage and ferocious, felt old depths of soul formerly containing wrath opening once more.

**Marius's pursuit and Valjean's withdrawal (Summer Year 5)**: Marius followed Cosette to Rue de l'Ouest. Spoke to porter. Porter reported to Valjean. **One week later, Valjean bestowed on Marius that glance which Marius at last perceived.** Valjean swore to himself never again to set foot in Luxembourg or Rue de l'Ouest. **Returned permanently to Rue Plumet.**

**Valjean's anguish over Cosette's transformation**: Recognizes Cosette escaping from him. Suffers greatly, becomes puerile; unconquerable conviction that Cosette is slipping away. Wishes to resist, retain her. Once envied General Comte Coutard on horseback, fantasized putting on uniform so Cosette would be dazzled. Contemplates cloister with despairing ecstasy; regrets abnegation in bringing Cosette back into world. Passes whole nights asking "What has Cosette in her mind?" Experiences grave significance of her silence: she says nothing, asks no questions, seeks not his reasons, already afraid of being divined and betraying herself.

**October 1831 morning routine**: Rise early before daybreak; trips planned on preceding evening—he proposed, she agreed, arranged like plot. Innocent eccentricities pleasing to young people. Matutinal walks equivalent to night stroll with added cheerfulness of nature; streets deserted, birds singing. Cosette a bird herself, liked to rise early. **In poor meadows**: Valjean loved haunt for solitude; liberty offered Cosette. She became little girl once more, ran and almost played. Took off hat, gathered bunches of flowers. Gazed at butterflies but did not catch them; wove garlands of poppies, placed on head, glowing until they flamed, formed crown of burning embers.

## Cosette's Coming of Age and Hidden Love (Summer Year 5—October 1831)
**Physical transformation complete**: Beautiful for tolerably long time before aware; consciousness of beauty burst upon her like sudden daylight. Skin white, hair lustrous, blue eyes gained unaccustomed splendor. Lost grace of ignoring beauty; gained pensive serious charm. Whole person permeated with joy of youth; innocence and beauty breathed forth splendid melancholy.

**Coquetry awakened and appearance changed**: Conceived horror for merinos, shame for plush hat. Father never refused anything. Acquired whole science of bonnet, gown, mantle, boot, cuff, stuff in fashion. First outing in new attire: black damask gown, white crape bonnet, gay, radiant, rosy, proud, dazzling. Valjean replied "Charming!" in voice resembling bitter envious man.

**Love for Marius**: Two souls prepared—Cosette in her shadow, Marius in his, charged and languishing with stormy electricity of passion. When their eyes met at last, Cosette did not immediately understand. Returned thoughtfully to Rue de l'Ouest house. Next morning: Thought of strange young man now paying attention to her. Assessed him: beautiful hair, eyes, teeth, charming tone, seemed noble, gentle, simple, proud, though poor. One day said to Valjean: "Father, let us stroll about a little in that direction." When Marius did not come to her, she went to him.

**Passionate ignorance**: First felt confused profound melancholy; soul seemed blackened. Did not know what love was; never heard word in terrestrial sense. **Loved with all passion because loved ignorantly.** Did not know whether good/bad, useful/dangerous, eternal/temporary, allowable/prohibited; loved. Loved without name, fault, spot, exigence, defect. He was not lover, not even admirer—vision. Set herself to adoring Marius as charming, luminous, impossible. Distant lover lingering in ideal, chimæra with form. Had all fears of children and nuns combined; convent spirit still slowly evaporating.

**October 1831 transformation and Valjean's withdrawal**: After Valjean bestowed that glance, Marius ceased coming to Luxembourg or Rue de l'Ouest. Cosette did not complain, said nothing, asked no questions, sought not Valjean's reasons. Already afraid of being divined, of betraying herself. The early-morning meadows excursions became her consolation—she became little girl once more, played, gathered flowers, wove garlands.

## Marius Pontmercy: Psychological and Financial Crisis
**Identity**: Baron Marius Pontmercy, twenty years old; three years estranged from grandfather. Paternal legacy: Colonel's instruction regarding Waterloo sergeant Thénardier.

**Financial crisis (Spring-Summer Year 5)**: **First time in life, borrowed five francs from Courfeyrac; now borrows hundred-sou piece (five francs).** Poverty returned; felt icy breath. Cannot focus on work—turning celebrated German quarrel into French. Cannot focus: reads four lines, attempts to write one, sees star between himself and paper.

**Psychological state**: Passion precipitated him into chimæras without object or bottom. Lost faculty of working toward fixed goal but endowed with more clear-sightedness and rectitude than ever. Judgment almost wholly disassociated from hope. Meditation turns to reproach; reflects dolefully on idleness, paralysis of soul gaining on him, night growing more dense. Happy, even in anguish.

**Change in demeanor and secret**: Once long indifferent and icy toward Cosette, now pays attention; wears new coat daily, uncertain whether has hair curled, wears gloves, exhibits awkward unnatural behavior—all observed and detested by Valjean. **Periodical five francs a double riddle**: to Courfeyrac who lent, to unknown recipient (Cosette) who received.

## Éponine's Reconnaissance (Year 5)
**Status**: Released from Les Madelonettes. Magnon handed Brujon's note. Went to Rue Plumet, recognized gate and garden, observed house, spied, lurked. Brought biscuit (prison symbol) to Magnon, transmitted to Babet's mistress. Network spreading, prison communication via "postilion"—moulded bread pallet sent rooftop courtyard-to-courtyard with notes.

## The Chain-Gang Procession (October 1831 Morning—Barrière du Maine)
**The vision**: October morning, Valjean and Cosette at break of day near Barrière du Maine. Valjean sitting in cross-walk on planks at timber-yard gate, sunk into profound absorption, thinking of Cosette, happiness possible if nothing came between them. Cosette standing beside him, gazing at clouds turning rosy. At elbow of causeway and inner boulevard, heard noise difficult to account for at that hour. **Gradually appeared seven chariots in succession**, horses touching rear of wagon in front. Figures moving on vehicles, flashes visible as though naked swords there, clanking audible resembling rattling of chains. Sound of voices waxed louder.

**The revelation**: As it drew nearer, assumed form, outlined behind trees with pallid hue of apparition. Mass grew white; daylight cast wan light on swarming heap at once sepulchral and living. **It was the chain-gang, which had set out before daybreak from Bicêtre, taken road to Mans in order to avoid Fontainebleau, where the King then was.** This caused horrible journey to last three or four days longer. Procession so long that when first vehicle reached barrier, last was barely emerging from boulevard. Throng sprung from nowhere, formed in twinkling, pressed forward from both sides. Neighboring lanes heard shouts of people calling and wooden shoes of market-gardeners hastening up.

**The spectacle of horror**: Mournful procession evident: rain might descend, men would not get dry again, once chilled would not get warm, linen trousers glued to bones, water filling shoes, lashes from whips unable to prevent jaws chattering, chain continuing to bind by neck, legs continuing to dangle. Impossible not to shudder at sight of human beings thus bound and passive beneath cold clouds of autumn, delivered over to rain, blast, all furies of air. Songs and blasphemies increased. Captain of escort cracked whip; fearful dull blind flogging produced sound of hail, fell upon seven dray-loads. Many roared and foamed at mouth; redoubled delight of street urchins, swarm of flies on wounds.

**Valjean's traumatic response (Excerpt 1117)**: Jean Valjean's eyes assumed frightful expression. No longer eyes; those deep glassy objects replacing glance in wretched men, seeming unconscious of reality, flames reflecting terrors and catastrophes. Not looking at spectacle, seeing vision. Tried to rise, flee, make escape; could not move feet. Remained nailed to spot, petrified, stupid, asking what sepulchral persecution signified, whence came pandemonium pursuing him. All at once raised hand to brow, gesture habitual to those whose memory suddenly returns; **remembered this was customary itinerary, customary to make this detour to avoid encountering royalty on road to Fontainebleau, and that thirty-five years before, he had himself passed through that barrier.**

**Cosette's reaction and return**: During journey back to Rue de Babylone, Cosette plied Valjean with questions on subject of what they had just seen; perhaps he was too much absorbed in own dejection to notice her words. But when Cosette was leaving him in evening to betake herself to bed, he heard her say in low voice, as though talking to herself: "It seems to me, that if I were to find one of those men in my pathway, oh, my God, I should die merely from the sight of him close at hand."

## Valjean's Illness and Renewed Intimacy (October 1831—November 1831)
**The Jondrette visit and wound**: At this epoch they paid visit to Jondrette den. **Day following that visit, Jean Valjean made appearance in pavilion in morning, calm as was his wont, but with large wound on left arm which was much inflamed and very angry, resembling burn, which he explained in some way or other.** This wound resulted in his being detained in house for a month with fever. He would not call in doctor. When Cosette urged him, "Call the dog-doctor," said he.

**Cosette's devotion**: Cosette on perceiving that her father was ill, had deserted pavilion and again taken fancy to little lodging and back courtyard. Passed nearly all her days beside Jean Valjean and read to him books which he desired. Generally they were books of travel. **Jean Valjean was undergoing a new birth; his happiness was reviving in these ineffable rays; the Luxembourg, the prowling young stranger, Cosette's coldness,—all these clouds upon his soul were growing dim. He had reached point where he said to himself: "I imagined all that. I am an old fool."**

**Charitable diversion**: One diversion, which had formerly been happiness, remained to them: carry bread to those hungry, clothing to those cold. Cosette often accompanied Jean Valjean on visits to poor, on which they recovered some remnants of their former free intercourse; sometimes when day had been good and they had assisted many in distress, Cosette was rather merry in evening.

**Thénardier discovery and acceptance**: His happiness so great that horrible discovery of Thénardiers made in Jondrette hovel, unexpected as it was, had glided over him unnoticed. **He had succeeded in making escape; all trace of him was lost—what more did he care for!** He only thought of those wretched beings to pity them. "Here they are in prison, and henceforth they will be incapacitated for doing any harm," he thought, "but what a lamentable family in distress!"
